content: The prevalence of obesity among children and adolescents has risen globally, leading to significant health consequences both in the short and long term. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of pharmacological treatments for obesity in this population. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of drugs, both licensed and unlicensed for obesity treatment, in individuals under 18 years of age. These trials required a minimum of three months of drug intervention and at least six months of follow-up. Studies involving eating disorders, type 2 diabetes, syndromic or secondary causes of obesity, growth hormone therapies, or pregnant participants were excluded. The review analyzed 21 trials, with a total of 2,484 participants. Of these, 1,478 were assigned to drug intervention groups, and 904 were in comparator groups. The drugs studied included metformin (11 trials), sibutramine (6 trials), orlistat (4 trials), and one trial that combined metformin with fluoxetine. Additionally, eight ongoing trials were identified, investigating metformin, topiramate, and exenatide. Most trials used a placebo as the comparator, and the intervention periods ranged from 12 to 48 weeks, with follow-up durations extending from six months to 100 weeks. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in body mass index (BMI), weight, and adverse events. All 21 trials measured these outcomes. Secondary outcomes included health-related quality of life, body fat distribution, behavior change, participants' perspectives on the intervention, morbidity, all-cause mortality, and socioeconomic effects. However, data on many secondary outcomes were limited or not reported. The results showed that pharmacological interventions led to modest reductions in BMI and weight. Specifically, the mean difference (MD) in BMI change was -1.3 kg/m² (95% confidence interval [CI] -1.9 to -0.8; P < 0.00001) across 16 trials involving 1,884 participants. When analyzed by drug type, sibutramine, metformin, and orlistat all demonstrated reductions in BMI compared to comparators. Similarly, the MD for weight change was -3.9 kg (95% CI -5.9 to -1.9; P < 0.00001) across 11 trials with 1,180 participants, with all three drugs showing weight reductions in favor of the intervention. Adverse events were reported in five trials, with serious adverse events occurring in 2.7% of participants in the intervention groups compared to 1.7% in the comparator groups (risk ratio [RR] 1.43, 95% CI 0.63 to 3.25). Trial discontinuation due to adverse events was higher in the intervention groups (5.0%) compared to the comparator groups (2.7%) (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.83 to 2.52). The most common adverse events associated with orlistat and metformin were gastrointestinal issues, such as diarrhea, mild abdominal pain, and fatty stools. Sibutramine trials frequently reported tachycardia, constipation, and hypertension. The single fluoxetine trial noted dry mouth and loose stools. The quality of the included trials was generally low, with many studies having a high risk of bias in at least one domain, short intervention periods, or limited follow-up. Dropout rates were high, with an overall rate of 25%. Furthermore, many of the drugs studied are not approved for obesity treatment in children and adolescents, and some, such as sibutramine, have been withdrawn from the market due to safety concerns. The authors concluded that pharmacological treatments, including metformin, sibutramine, orlistat, and fluoxetine, may result in small reductions in BMI and body weight in obese children and adolescents. However, the evidence is of low certainty, and the long-term safety and efficacy of these interventions remain unclear. Future research should prioritize high-quality trials with adequate sample sizes, long-term follow-up, and standardized reporting of adverse events. Regulatory requirements for pediatric trials by agencies such as the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) should encourage the development of more robust evidence in this area.
